357:                                    Integrating experiments and simulations
358:                                    While the MD simulations are overall in good agreement with the SAXS and NMR NOE data, there
359:                                    remain discrepancies that could contain information about the conformational ensemble of DH5-
360:                                    DMPC in solution. We therefore used a previously described Bayesian/Maximum Entropy (BME)
361:                                    approach (Hummer and Köfinger, 2015; Różycki et al., 2011; Bottaro et al., 2018; Cesari et al.,
362:                                    2016; Bottaro et al., 2020) to integrate the MD simulations with the SAXS and NMR data. Briefly,
363:                                    the BME method refines the simulation against measured experimental averages by balancing (1)
364:                                    minimizing the discrepancy between the simulation and the observed experimental averages and (2)
365:                                    ensuring as little perturbation of the original simulation as possible thereby limiting chances of over-
366:                                    fitting. The outcome is a conformational ensemble that is more likely to represent DH5-DMPC in
367:                                    solution. In practice, this is achieved by changing the weight of each configuration in the ensemble
368:                                    obtained from the MD simulations, and we therefore call this a ‘reweighted ensemble’ (Bottaro and
369:                                    Lindorff-Larsen, 2018; Bottaro et al., 2020). The amount of reweighting can be quantified by an
370:                                    entropy change (Srel ) that reports on how much the weights had to be changed to fit the data
371:                                    (Bottaro et al., 2018) (see Materials and methods). Alternatively, the value feff ¼ expðSrel Þ reports
372:                                    on the effective ensemble size, that is what fraction of the original frames that were used to derive
373:                                    the final ensemble (Orioli et al., 2020). We note that we reweight each individual conformation in
374:                                    the ensemble, and thus that the clustering is only used for presenting the results. In this way we
375:                                    avoid uncertainties that come from difficulties in clustering heterogeneous ensembles.
376:                                        We used both the SAXS and NOE data individually, as well as combined, to understand the
377:                                    effects of each source of data on the reweighted conformational ensemble (Table 2). We note that
378:                                    when a specific type of data is used to generate the ensemble, the resulting c2 simply reports on
379:                                    how well the simulation has been fitted to the data; because of the maximum-entropy regularization
380:                                    to avoid overfitting, we do not fit the data as accurately as possible. The two types of experimental
381:                                    data complement each other in structural information content. Specifically, the SAXS data report on
382:                                    the overall size and shape, and is sensitive to both protein and lipids through atom-atom pair distri-
383:                                    butions in a range starting from » 10 Å, whereas the NOEs contain local, specific atom-atom distan-
384:                                    ces from the protein belts of the DH5 but not any direct information about the lipids.
385:                                        We find that refining against a single of the two data types only improves the MD trajectory with
386:                                    respect to the structural properties it is sensitive to, highlighting the orthogonal information in the
387:                                    two sources of information. In addition, we performed reweighting with the methyl NOEs and the
388:                                    amide NOEs separately (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). The already low discrepancy of the amide
389:                                    NOEs barely improves while the discrepancies of both methyl NOEs and SAXS are unaffected by
390:                                    integration with amide NOEs alone, implying that the structural information content contained in the
391:                                    amide NOEs (mostly secondary structure) is already correctly captured by the force field and starting
392:                                    structure. Because the NOE and SAXS experiments provide independent information we refined the
393:                                    ensemble against both sets of data (Figure 3). We find that we can fit both sources of data at rea-
394:                                    sonable accuracy without dramatic changes of the weights away from the Boltzmann distribution of
395:                                    the force field (feff ¼ 18%).
396:                                        Finally, we used the PRE and EPR data to validate the refined ensemble. In general we find com-
397:                                    parable and overall good agreement between the original NMR/EPR structure and our MD refined

399:                                    directly as input in the refinement (Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and Figure 2—figure supple-

5: # Are We Capturing the Ensemble?
6: 
7: 
8: ### What structural biology experiments preserve, blur, or discard about molecular distributions
9: 
10: 
11: Minhuan Li, F. Emil Thomasen, Pilar Cossio{minhuanli,fthomasen,pcossio}@flatironinstitute.org
12: 
13: 
14: 
15: 
16: Two ways in which an experiment can encode a conformational ensemble. Ensemble-averaged measurements combine contributions from many molecules into each observable. In single-particle measurements, each observation arises from an individual molecule, and the ensemble is represented statistically across many observations.
17: 
18: 
19: 
20: Structural biology is increasingly being asked to answer questions about ensembles rather than single structures. But two opposite intuitions can lead us astray. In cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), a fuzzy or weak region of a reconstructed map is sometimes treated as if it were direct evidence of an ensemble: blur becomes heterogeneity. In the other direction, an experiment such as X-ray diffraction may be dismissed as incapable of constraining an ensemble because its measurements average over many molecules.
21: 
22: 
23: 
24: These intuitions seem contradictory, but they make the same mistake. Both assume what an experiment can tell us about a molecular distribution from the appearance of its final representation, rather than from how the data were generated or processed. A blurred map is not itself an ensemble distribution. But neither does averaging an observable necessarily collapse a distribution to a single structure.
25: 
26: 
27: 
28: The more useful question is therefore not whether a dataset “contains an ensemble”. It is which differences between molecular distributions remain observable after measurement and subsequent data processing. Two distinct ensembles may produce measurably different signals, or they may become indistinguishable once corrupted by experimental noise, limited by partially projected observables or finite sampling, nuisance variables, or distorted by data processing steps.
29: 
30: 
31: 
32: To make this precise, we first need to distinguish the distribution we ideally would like to learn from the one the experiment actually sees.
33: 
34: 
35: 
36: ### What distribution enters the experiment?
37: 
38: 
39: 
40: Before asking what information the measurement pipeline preserves, we should first be clear about what distribution is being measured. Let \(p_{\mathrm{target}}(x)\) denote a molecular distribution relevant to the scientific question, and \(p_{\mathrm{src}}(x)\) the source distribution actually present in the prepared sample when the measurement is made. We refer to \(p_{\mathrm{src}}\) as the molecular ensemble distribution—the distribution we can, in principle, attempt to measure and infer. Often we hope that \(p_{\mathrm{src}}\) faithfully represents \(p_{\mathrm{target}}\), but the two need not be identical.
41: 
42: 
43: 
44: The distinction is especially concrete in cryo-EM, where vitrification is itself a physical process acting on the ensemble. Recent work by Clark et al. examined how rapid cooling can perturb conformational populations and how equilibrium populations might subsequently be inferred from the vitrified ensemble [6]. More generally, temperature, chemical environment, sample preparation, and experimental timescales can all affect the relationship between the distribution of biological interest and the one presented to the instrument.
45: 
46: 
47: 
48: The possible difference between \(p_{\mathrm{target}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{src}}\) is important, but it is not the problem we will pursue here. We will take the source distribution as the object presented to the experiment and ask what happens next:
49: 
50: \[p_{\mathrm{src}}\longrightarrow\text{measurements}\longrightarrow\text{processed data}.\]
51: 
52: 
53: 
54: Which distinctions within \(p_{\mathrm{src}}\) survive this chain?
55: 
56: 
57: 
58: ### How experiments constrain the source distribution
59: 
60: 
61: 
62: Different experiments encode \(p_{\mathrm{src}}\) in different ways. Broadly, there are two cases. In an ensemble-averaged measurement, each observable combines contributions from many molecules. In a single-molecule measurement, individual observations arise from individual molecules, and the distribution appears statistically across many observations. These are not rankings of how much “ensemble information” an experiment contains. They are different ways of gaining information about the underlying distribution.
63: 
64: 
65: 
66: For an ensemble-average measurement, in its simplest form, the observable can be written as
67: 
68: \[y = \int m(x, z)\,\pi(z)\,p_{\mathrm{src}}(x)\,dx\,dz + \varepsilon,\]
69: 
70: 
71: 
72: where \(m(\cdot)\) is the forward model for the observable, \(z\) collects experimental nuisance variables (for example molecule poses) with distribution \(\pi(z)\), and \(\varepsilon\) represents measurement uncertainty. The experiment doesn’t measure the observable for any individual molecule. Instead, it reports the expectation value of that observable over the source distribution and the nuisance variables.
73: 
74: 
75: 
76: Importantly, averaging in observable space is not the same as averaging in conformational space. Suppose two conformations, \(x_A\) and \(x_B\), occur with probabilities \(p_A\) and \(p_B\). Suppressing the nuisance variables, the measured signal is \(p_A m(x_A)+p_B m(x_B)\), not, in general, \(m\left(p_A x_A+p_B x_B\right)\). This distinction matters. If the observable responds differently to the two conformations, their contributions can remain separately constrained even though the measurement averages over many molecules. X-ray diffraction intensities, for example, need not correspond to a fictitious structure halfway between two populated conformations. Spatially distinct states can leave distinct contributions to the measured density. “Averaged” therefore does not mean “only informative about an average structure.”
77: 
78: 
79: 
80: Single-particle experiments preserve a different kind of information. We can describe an individual observation as arising from a latent molecular state,
81: 
82: \[x_n \sim p_{\mathrm{src}}(x),\]
83: 
84: 
85: 
86: together with experimental nuisance variables \(z_n\), followed by a measurement process described by the distribution \(K\),
87: 
88: \[y_n \sim K(\cdot \mid x_n,z_n)\,.\]
89: 
90: 
91: 
92: In single-molecule FRET, time traces of the same molecule can reveal transitions between coarse conformational states. In single-particle cryo-EM, time is not preserved: each particle contributes a noisy projection of one molecular configuration, and the ensemble appears through variation across many different particles.
93: 
94: 
95: 
96: For independent observations, their marginal distribution is
97: 
98: \[p(y) = \int K(y\mid x,z)\,\pi(z)\,p_{\mathrm{src}}(x)\,dz\,dx.\]
99:
